title: Assignment 2: Google Trends, Two Ways
text:
Data sheet: primary website query



Terms: Trump, Kamala Harris, Election (each selected as a search term, not a topic)
Geography: United States (US) · Window: past five years (today+5-y)
Category: all (0) · Search type: Web Search (web)
Pulled: 2026-09-12 16:38:24 CDT
Query: Google Trends Explore
The website CSV covers 2021-09-12 through 2026-09-06 at weekly intervals. With the same three terms but a 90-day window, the CSV covers 2026-06-12 through 2026-09-12 daily. Thus, Google changed the time resolution with the window. My additional current-news term was Federal Reserve (US, past 90 days, all categories, Web Search), pulled 2026-09-12 16:39:35 CDT; the term was timely because an FOMC meeting was scheduled for September 15–16 (Federal Reserve calendar).

title: Assignment 2: Google Trends, Two Ways
text:
R pull and comparison


Code
library(gtrendsR)
library(readr)

r_pull <- gtrends(
  c("Trump", "Kamala Harris", "Election"),
  onlyInterest = TRUE, geo = "US", gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y", category = 0
)
write_csv(r_pull$interest_over_time,
          "data/r_trump_kamala-election_us_5y_2026-09-12.csv")




Code
ggplot(web, aes(date, hits, color = keyword)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.55) +
  geom_point(data = r |> group_by(keyword) |> slice(seq(1, n(), by = 13)),
             shape = 21, fill = "white", size = 1.7, stroke = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~keyword, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#2A9D8F", "#6C5CE7", "#E76F51")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Google Trends index (0–100)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "none", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())





Figure 1: Weekly Google search-interest index. Lines are the website CSV; open points are every thirteenth gtrendsR observation. Exact overlap means the two pulls matched in this run.




After mapping the website’s <1 cells to zero, all 783 aligned observations were identical: mean absolute difference 0, maximum difference 0, and therefore no direction of difference. The raw files are still structurally different: the website is wide, uses Week and <1, and puts the category in a preamble; R is long and adds query metadata to every row. This is a result of these particular pulls, not a guarantee.
Google Trends is not a count. Google says it samples searches, divides each point by total searches for its time and geography, and rescales within the query from 0 to 100. Thus 100 is the query’s peak relative interest; 0 generally means too little volume to report, not necessarily no searches. Google also cautions that Trends is not polling and that a spike does not mean a topic is “winning” (Google Trends FAQ).

title: Assignment 2: Google Trends, Two Ways
text:
Sensitivity and method choice
Removing Kamala Harris and rerunning the five-year website query changed 67 of 522 remaining observations (12.8%). Every changed cell rose in the two-term pull; the largest increase was four index points. This happens because the sample and the within-query normalization are recomputed, so values are comparable only inside the query that produced them.
Harris and Kamala Harris were not the same series: in a joint R query none of their 261 weekly values matched; the mean absolute gap was 7.46 and the maximum was 35 index points. A search term measures the literal words entered, whereas a Google Trends topic groups searches for a concept across wording and languages (Google’s term-versus-topic guide). The bare surname therefore does not isolate the intended person.
The website is transparent to inspect but manual: its interest-over-time CSV records the category plus term/geography labels, while my separate query log had to preserve the time window, search type, term-versus-topic choice, and pull time. The R output records keyword, geo, time, gprop, and category in every row and scales to many scripted terms, countries, and repetitions. Neither route guarantees identical future values, but R makes the procedure far easier to regenerate. It is also fragile: gtrendsR depends on an unofficial endpoint, so rate limits or a changed response can break a call; my first website load returned HTTP 429 before a retry succeeded. I cache the first success, retain the raw RDS/CSV, and check row counts, date ranges, and missing values.
With onlyInterest = FALSE, names(tct) returned interest_over_time plus interest_by_country, interest_by_region, interest_by_dma, interest_by_city, related_topics, and related_queries. The single website chart download contained only the first; the other six were absent. The package documents these list-based results and the onlyInterest switch (gtrendsR reference manual).
I also completed and cached the required extensions: Taylor Swift over time = "all", the same term in Great Britain, the term across c("US", "GB", "TW"), and Taylor Swift, Beyonce, and Adele worldwide.
Finally, two identical Federal Reserve R calls returned the same 93 daily values in this run. Because Google describes Trends as sampled data with small statistical noise, equality once does not establish stability. Any reported finding should archive its exact pull, be checked with repetitions, and avoid overinterpreting small differences (Google Trends FAQ).
The complete cached workflow is in code/gtrendsR01.R; derived comparisons are produced by code/analyze_trends.R.

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
For this assignment, I use the 2024 American Community Survey (ACS) five-year estimates to look at how income and poverty vary across Texas counties. I map median household income and rank counties by poverty rate. I use a rate instead of the number of people below poverty because a count would mostly reflect differences in county population size.






Geography and variables




Geography: Texas counties
Median household income: B19013_001
Population below poverty: B17001_002
Population for whom poverty status was determined: B17001_001
Survey: 2024 ACS five-year estimates (acs5)



The Census API key was installed once in .Renviron; it is not stored in this document or in the public repository.

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
Variable metadata and data retrieval
I first check the variable codes against the 2024 ACS five-year metadata. The current tidycensus interface loads the metadata directly from the Census API, so I do not use the deprecated cache argument.


Code
vars <- load_variables(2024, "acs5")

vars |>
  filter(name %in% c("B19013_001", "B17001_001", "B17001_002")) |>
  select(name, label, concept) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Variable", "Label", "Concept"),
    align = c("l", "l", "l")
  )




Table 1: ACS variables used in the analysis.







Variable
Label
Concept




B17001_001
Estimate!!Total:
Poverty Status in the Past 12 Months by Sex by Age


B17001_002
Estimate!!Total:!!Income in the past 12 months below poverty level:
Poverty Status in the Past 12 Months by Sex by Age


B19013_001
Estimate!!Median household income in the past 12 months (in 2024 inflation-adjusted dollars)
Median Household Income in the Past 12 Months (in 2024 Inflation-Adjusted Dollars)






The next call downloads the estimates, margins of error, and county geometry in wide form. In the resulting column names, E identifies an estimate and M identifies its margin of error.


Code
state_abbr <- "TX"
geo_level <- "county"
year_acs <- 2024
survey_name <- "acs5"

my_vars <- c(
  income = "B19013_001",
  pov = "B17001_002",
  povden = "B17001_001"
)

acs_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = geo_level,
  variables = my_vars,
  state = state_abbr,
  year = year_acs,
  survey = survey_name,
  geometry = TRUE,
  output = "wide"
)

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
section: Constructing the poverty rate and uncertainty interval
text:
Constructing the poverty rate and uncertainty interval
I calculate the poverty rate by dividing the estimated number of people below poverty by the estimated population for whom poverty status was determined. Because both values come from a sample, I carry their uncertainty into the rate with moe_prop(). ACS margins of error are reported at the 90% confidence level, so I construct each interval as the estimate plus or minus its MOE.


Code
acs_wide <- acs_wide |>
  mutate(
    pov_rate = povE / povdenE,
    pov_rate_moe = moe_prop(povE, povdenE, povM, povdenM),
    pov_ci_low = pmax(0, pov_rate - pov_rate_moe),
    pov_ci_high = pmin(1, pov_rate + pov_rate_moe)
  )

stopifnot(
  nrow(acs_wide) == 254,
  !anyNA(acs_wide$incomeE),
  !anyNA(acs_wide$pov_rate),
  all(acs_wide$povdenE > 0)
)

write_csv(
  st_drop_geometry(acs_wide),
  "data/acs_TX_county_2024.csv"
)

Median household income map


Code
ggplot(acs_wide) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = incomeE), color = "white", linewidth = 0.08) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "C",
    name = "Median household\nincome (2024 $)",
    labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1, big.mark = ",")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Household Income by County in Texas",
    subtitle = "ACS 2024 five-year estimates",
    caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau via tidycensus."
  ) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.position = "right"
  )





Figure 1: Median household income across Texas counties. Values are ACS 2024 five-year estimates.




Estimated median household income ranges from $36,165 to $127,981. Rockwall and Collin counties are at the high end of the distribution. Swisher, Zavala, Starr, Dimmit, and Zapata counties are among those at the low end. This map shows where the estimates are higher or lower, but it does not explain what caused those differences.

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
Poverty-rate ranking
Before ranking the counties, I remove the geometry and keep the full-precision values for all calculations. I round only the numbers displayed in the table. The poverty-rate estimate and its MOE are both reported in percentage points.


Code
poverty_data <- acs_wide |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(!is.na(pov_rate), !is.na(pov_rate_moe), povdenE > 0)

top10 <- poverty_data |>
  arrange(desc(pov_rate)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  mutate(group = "Highest 10")

bottom10 <- poverty_data |>
  arrange(pov_rate) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  mutate(group = "Lowest 10")

ranked_table <- bind_rows(top10, bottom10) |>
  group_by(group) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number()) |>
  ungroup()

table_for_display <- ranked_table |>
  transmute(
    Group = group,
    Rank = rank,
    County = sub(", Texas$", "", NAME),
    `Poverty rate` = scales::percent(pov_rate, accuracy = 0.1),
    `MOE` = scales::percent(pov_rate_moe, accuracy = 0.1),
    `90% confidence interval` = paste0(
      scales::percent(pov_ci_low, accuracy = 0.1),
      " to ",
      scales::percent(pov_ci_high, accuracy = 0.1)
    )
  )

knitr::kable(
  table_for_display,
  col.names = c(
    "Group", "Rank", "County", "Poverty rate",
    "MOE", "90% confidence interval"
  ),
  align = c("l", "r", "l", "r", "r", "r")
)

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
Uncertainty check


Code
overlap_example <- ranked_table |>
  filter(NAME %in% c("Dimmit County, Texas", "Zapata County, Texas")) |>
  transmute(
    County = sub(", Texas$", "", NAME),
    Estimate = scales::percent(pov_rate, accuracy = 0.1),
    MOE = scales::percent(pov_rate_moe, accuracy = 0.1),
    `90% confidence interval` = paste0(
      scales::percent(pov_ci_low, accuracy = 0.1),
      " to ",
      scales::percent(pov_ci_high, accuracy = 0.1)
    )
  )

knitr::kable(overlap_example, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"))

Dimmit County’s 90% confidence interval is 32.2% to 50.0%, and Zapata County’s is 32.4% to 44.4%. These intervals overlap substantially. Dimmit ranks above Zapata when I use the point estimates, but the ACS sampling uncertainty means that I cannot confidently conclude that Dimmit’s underlying poverty rate is higher. I therefore treat the table as a ranking of estimates rather than a precise ordering of the counties’ true rates.

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
Methods note
For this project, I use the 2024 ACS five-year estimates for all 254 Texas counties. I map median household income (B19013_001) and calculate poverty rates by dividing the estimated population below poverty (B17001_002) by the population for whom poverty status was determined (B17001_001). This rate is more useful for comparing counties than a count, which is strongly affected by population size. I use moe_prop() to carry the numerator and denominator margins of error into the poverty rate, and I report 90% confidence intervals. Dimmit and Zapata counties rank first and second by their point estimates, but their intervals overlap. This overlap means that the data do not clearly establish which county has the higher underlying poverty rate. I therefore interpret the table as a descriptive ranking rather than an exact ordering. Data were retrieved from the U.S. Census Bureau through tidycensus.

title: Assignment 3: ACS via tidycensus
text:
Reproducibility
The analysis retrieves the estimates and geometry from the Census API. I also save a geometry-free copy of the complete dataset as data/acs_TX_county_2024.csv. The CSV includes the original estimates and MOEs, the derived poverty rate and its propagated MOE, and the lower and upper limits of the 90% confidence interval.
